name: Edelrid Kurt Haulbag
title: Edelrid Kurt Haulbag: Climbing Haul Bag for Tree Work
meta: The Edelrid Kurt is a tough climbing haul bag for moving rope, hardware and saddles from the truck to the tree. Typical price, uses and buying notes inside.
tagline: A rugged climbing haul bag for climbers who carry a full kit to every job.
summary: The Edelrid Kurt Haulbag is a climbing haul bag built to take a beating on the ground, in the truck and on the drop zone. It swallows a climb line, hitch cords and a rack of hardware in one load, so your kit shows up at the tree together.
highlights: Heavy-duty haul bag body that shrugs off bark, sawdust and truck beds
Big-volume body that swallows rope, saddle and hardware together
Carry straps for hauling kit across a yard or up to a lift
Keeps climbing gear off wet ground and away from fuel and bar oil
Simple, open layout that is easy to dump out and inspect
specs: Storage and transport, not life support

body.h: What it does on a job
p: Most climbers end up with a pile of gear that lives loose in a truck box: rope bags, a saddle, a few lanyards, a bucket of carabiners. A haul bag puts all of it in one place. Load the Kurt at the shop, throw it on your back at the job and dump it on a tarp at the base of the tree.

Because it is built like a big-wall bag, it holds up to being dragged through brush and set down on mulch, gravel and wet lawns. That matters, because contaminants like bar oil, gas and grit are what shorten the life of rope and textiles.

A haul bag also makes the start of the day faster. Instead of digging through a truck box for the right lanyard or the spare hitch cord, you grab one bag and know everything is in it. At the end of the job, everything goes back in before you leave the site, which cuts down on gear left behind at the base of a tree.

It suits climbers who move between crews or trucks and want their personal kit to stay together, and anyone who is tired of rope bags splitting at the seams. If you only carry a single line and a few biners, a smaller rope bag from our gear bags section may be enough.
Keep life-support gear clean and dry between jobs, and keep your inspection routine the same no matter how you store it.

Before buying, think about what you actually carry. A full saddle, a long climb line and a hardware rack take real volume, and a bag that is packed to bursting is slow to load and hard on zippers and seams.

faq.q: Can I store my saddle and rope in the same haul bag?
faq.a: Yes, as long as everything is clean and dry. Keep sharp tools, files and fuel out of the bag so they cannot damage textiles.

faq.q: Is a haul bag better than a rope bag?
faq.a: A rope bag is built to feed rope cleanly. A haul bag is built to carry a whole kit. Many climbers use a rope bag inside a haul bag.

name: Petzl Duffel 85L Gear Bag
title: Petzl Duffel 85L Backpack Gear Bag for Arborists
meta: The Petzl Duffel 85L is an 85L backpack-style duffel that hauls a complete climbing kit. See capacity, typical price and how tree crews use it on the job.
tagline: An 85-liter duffel that carries like a backpack, sized for a full climbing kit.
summary: The Petzl Duffel 85L is a large gear bag that doubles as an 85L backpack, so you can carry a full tree climbing kit on your shoulders instead of in your arms. It is big enough for a saddle, a climb line, lanyards and a rack of hardware, with a wide opening that makes packing fast.
highlights: 85-liter capacity holds a saddle, rope and hardware in one load
Backpack straps for long walks from the truck to the tree
Wide zippered opening so you can see and reach everything
Coated, water-resistant fabric that wipes clean after a muddy job
Grab handles on the ends for loading trucks and chippers

body.h: Why an 85L backpack duffel makes sense for tree work
p: A climbing kit is bulky. Between a saddle, a 150-foot climb line, a rope bag, a flip line, a friction device and a dozen carabiners, you can easily fill 60 liters before you add a helmet or a spare layer. An 85L backpack duffel gives you room for all of it plus the odds and ends that usually get left in the truck.

The backpack straps are the real reason to choose this bag over a plain duffel. Residential jobs often mean a long walk through a backyard, around a pool and down a slope. Carrying 30 pounds of gear on your back is a lot easier than hauling it by a handle, and it leaves your hands free for a saw or a pole pruner.
When you are not carrying it far, the end handles make it easy to load into a truck box or behind a seat.

Size also helps on storm jobs and multi-day work. You can keep a dry base layer, a spare set of gloves and a headlamp in the same bag as your climbing kit, so a long day does not depend on what someone remembered to throw in the truck.

Put the saddle in first, flat against the back panel, then the rope bag on top. Hardware goes in a separate pouch so carabiner gates and pulleys do not chew on your textiles. Keep files, wedges and anything sharp in a different bag entirely.

Do not store wet gear in a closed duffel overnight. If you finish a job in the rain, open the bag at the shop and hang your rope and saddle to dry. Damp textiles packed tight can mildew, and that is a reason to retire life-support gear early.
Keep the bag away from fuel, bar oil and battery acid. Even a water-resistant liner can pick up contamination from a soaked truck bed.
Label the inside of the bag or your hardware pouch with your name. On crews where several climbers run similar gear, that saves arguments at the end of the day.

This bag suits climbers who travel between crews, storm-work climbers who live out of a truck for a week, and anyone who wants their whole personal kit in one place at the start of the day. It is also a good pick for climbing schools and trainers who move sets of gear between sites.

If you only need to carry rope, a dedicated rope bag that feeds line cleanly is the better tool. Many climbers keep a rope bag inside the duffel and pull it out at the tree. You can compare options in our gear bags and rope bags sections.
It is also a practical bag for storing a backup kit at the shop, ready to grab when a climber's own gear is out for inspection or repair.
Shake out sawdust and leaves after each job, wipe down the coated fabric, and check the zipper for grit. A bit of zipper lubricant keeps it running smoothly in dusty conditions.
Storage is part of gear care, not a substitute for it. Inspect your rope, saddle and hardware before every climb, no matter how carefully it was packed.
If the zipper starts to separate behind the slider, a worn slider is usually the cause and can often be replaced before the whole bag is retired.

faq.q: Will a saddle and a 150-foot climb line fit in the 85L bag?
faq.a: Yes. An 85-liter bag holds a typical arborist saddle and a 150-foot line with room left over for lanyards, hardware and a helmet.

faq.q: Is the Petzl Duffel waterproof?
faq.a: The coated fabric is water-resistant and sheds rain and wet grass well, but it is not a submersible dry bag. Dry wet gear out of the bag.

faq.q: Can I carry it as a backpack all day?
faq.a: It is designed for carrying gear between the truck and the work site. For long hikes, a dedicated pack with a hip belt carries heavy loads more comfortably.

name: Courant Cross Rope Bag (23 / 36 L)
title: Courant Bag for Rope: Cross Rope Bag 23 L / 36 L
meta: The Courant Cross is a Courant bag built to store and feed climbing rope cleanly. Compare the 23 L and 36 L sizes, typical price and what each one holds.
tagline: A stand-up rope bag that keeps your climb line clean and feeds it without tangles.
summary: The Courant Cross rope bag is a Courant bag sized in 23 L and 36 L versions to hold a climbing line and feed it cleanly at the base of the tree. It keeps the line clean between climbs and makes stuffing rope at the end of the day quick.
highlights: Two sizes: 23 L for shorter lines, 36 L for longer or thicker lines
Open, simple layout that is fast to stuff at the end of a climb
Keeps the line out of sawdust, mud and the drop zone
Easy to carry from tree to tree on the job
specs: Storing and feeding a climb line

p: Rope bag volume is mostly about how long and how thick your line is. The 23 L Cross suits a shorter climb line or a single-rope access line for smaller trees. The 36 L size gives room for a longer 11.5 to 13 mm climbing line or a line plus a lanyard and a few carabiners.
If you are unsure, go bigger. A bag that is too small is slow to stuff, and rope crammed into a tight bag is more likely to come out in knots.

The 23 L version is also a tidy way to keep a lanyard, a short access line or a spare hitch cord kit separate from your main rope bag. Smaller bags are easier to clip to a saddle or tuck into a truck box, and they make it obvious at a glance what is inside.

body.h: How it helps on the job
p: A good rope bag keeps the line out of sawdust, mud and the path of the chipper. Secure the tail, flake the rope in loosely, and it will feed back out clean when you set your next anchor. The Cross is also a convenient way to keep separate lines for climbing and rigging, which you should never mix up.
Store your bag dry and inspect your rope before each climb. See more options in our rope bags section.

Wash the bag out now and then. Sawdust, sand and grit collect in the bottom and work their way into rope fibers every time you stuff the line back in. Shake it out after every job and rinse it when it gets dirty.

faq.q: How much rope fits in the 36 L Courant bag?
faq.a: Capacity depends on diameter and how loosely you stuff it. A 36 L bag comfortably holds a typical arborist climb line, while the 23 L version is better for shorter lines.

faq.q: Should I tie the rope tail inside the bag?
faq.a: Yes. Anchoring the tail keeps the end from running out of the bag and gives you a known stopping point when feeding line.

name: TreeHog 40L Rope Bag
title: Tree Hog 40L Rope Bag for Arborist Climb Lines
meta: The Tree Hog 40L rope bag holds a full arborist climb line and feeds it clean at the base of the tree. See what fits, typical price and how crews use it.
tagline: A 40-liter rope bag from TreeHog for climbers who run a full-length line.
summary: The Tree Hog 40L rope bag is a roomy, simple bag for storing and feeding an arborist climbing line. At 40 liters it holds a full-length climb line with space to spare, so stuffing rope at the end of the day goes fast.
highlights: 40-liter capacity for a full-length climb line
Wide mouth for quick stuffing and clean feeding
Keeps rope clean and organized between climbs
Easy to move from tree to tree

body.h: A rope bag that keeps up
p: Rope that lives in a pile on the ground picks up grit, gets stepped on and ends up in the brush pile. A 40L rope bag keeps the line together and clean. Secure the tail, flake the rope in loosely, and it feeds back out without kinks when you throw your next line.
The extra volume over a 25 or 30 liter bag means you are not fighting to close it, and there is space for a lanyard or a friction hitch cord on top.

TreeHog is known among climbers for simple, durable storage gear. This bag is not complicated: a big open body, a way to anchor the tail and handles to carry it. That simplicity is what you want from a rope bag you use every day and drag through every job site.
Mark the bag with tape or a tag that says what rope is in it and its diameter. When three bags sit at the base of a tree, nobody should have to guess which one holds the climb line.

body.h: Good habits with any rope bag
p: Keep climbing and rigging lines in separate, clearly marked bags. Do not store a wet rope sealed in a bag for days. Keep the bag away from fuel cans, bar oil and battery boxes in the truck.
A clean bag helps your rope last, but it does not replace inspection. Check your line before every climb. Browse more sizes in our rope bags section.
On storm jobs and long removals, it is also a handy place to stash a lowering line or a spare climb line so it stays ready and clean in the drop zone.

faq.q: Will a 150-foot climbing line fit in the TreeHog 40L?
faq.a: A 40-liter bag generally holds a typical 150-foot arborist climb line in common diameters, with some room left for a lanyard.

faq.q: Can I use it for rigging rope?
faq.a: You can, but keep rigging and climbing lines in separate, marked bags so a rigging line never ends up as a climb line.

name: Big Jim's Hitch Breaker
title: Big Jim's Hitch Breaker: Smoother Climbing Hitch Control
meta: Big Jim's Hitch Breaker helps you tend and release a friction hitch with less effort on MRS and SRS systems. How it works, who it suits and typical price.
tagline: A small tending aid for climbers who want a friction hitch that releases cleanly.
summary: Big Jim's Hitch Breaker is a compact tending aid that sits at the base of your friction hitch and gives you a solid point to break and release it. Climbers use the hitch breaker to make descents smoother and to keep the climbing hitch dressed and tended as they advance up the line.
highlights: Gives you a firm handle for breaking a loaded friction hitch
Helps keep the climbing hitch dressed and tended while advancing
Works with common eye-and-eye hitch cords
Small and light enough to live on your climbing system
Simple, no-moving-parts design that is easy to inspect
specs: Friction hitch tending and release aid
Moving rope (MRS) and stationary rope (SRS) hitch setups

p: Every friction hitch climber knows the moment: you have been sitting in the saddle, the hitch has bitten down hard, and now you need to move. Grabbing the top of a Distel or VT and pulling it down works, but it is fiddly with gloves on and it can lurch. A hitch breaker gives you a dedicated, rigid point at the base of the hitch to pull against, so the release is more gradual and controlled.

It also helps the hitch keep its shape. When a climbing hitch is tended from below, it stays dressed and is less likely to roll or creep out of position as you advance. That means less time re-dressing cord and more time working.

The breaker is not a replacement for a properly tied, properly sized hitch. Cord diameter, cord material, the number of wraps and the rope you are climbing on still decide how well the system grabs and releases.
Because it gives your hand a consistent place to work, the release becomes more repeatable, which is what helps most on long descents where you are feathering the hitch for minutes at a time.

Follow the instructions that come with the device for how it connects to your hitch cord and bridge, and match your cord and rope diameters to what the maker recommends. Build the system on the ground, load-test it at chest height, and check that the hitch grabs fully when you let go before you leave the ground.
If you are switching from a hitch-tending pulley, expect a short learning period. The release feels different, and you may want to adjust the number of wraps or the cord length to get the feel right.
Anything you hang your life on must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and be inspected before every climb by a trained user.
Expect to fine-tune the system over a few climbs. Small changes in cord length or wraps can make a noticeable difference in how the hitch feels when you break it.

It is popular with climbers who run a traditional friction hitch and want finer control on descent without moving to a mechanical device. It also suits newer climbers who struggle to break a tight hitch smoothly, provided they are learning under a qualified trainer.
Pair it with a quality eye-and-eye cord from our eye-and-eye prusiks section, or compare it with a hitch-tending pulley such as the DMM Hitch Climber.
Some climbers also like it for training days, because it makes the moment of release easier to see and explain to someone learning the hitch.

Check the device for burrs, sharp edges and grooving where cord or rope runs over it, and retire it if you find cracks or deformation. Inspect the hitch cord at the same time, paying attention to glazing, flat spots and stiff sections that come from heat during long descents.
Wipe sap and grit off the device after use. Contaminants on any surface the hitch contacts can change how the hitch grabs.

faq.q: Does a hitch breaker replace a hitch-tending pulley?
faq.a: It can, for climbers who want a simpler way to break and tend the hitch. A pulley tends slack more smoothly as you advance; a breaker focuses on control at the hitch. Some climbers prefer one, some the other.

faq.q: Which climbing hitch works best with it?
faq.a: It is generally used with common eye-and-eye hitches such as the Distel and Valdotain Tresse. Follow the maker's guidance and test the setup on the ground before climbing.

faq.q: Is it a life-support component?
faq.a: It sits in your climbing system, so treat it with the same care as any other part of it. Use it only as the manufacturer intends and inspect it before each climb.

name: DMM Hitch Climber Kit
title: DMM Hitch Climber Kit with Hitch Climber Pulley
meta: The DMM Hitch Climber kit pairs the Hitch Climber pulley with matched carabiners for a clean, tended friction hitch. What is included and typical price.
tagline: A matched hitch-tending pulley and connector set for building a friction hitch system.
summary: The DMM Hitch Climber kit bundles the Hitch Climber pulley with matching DMM carabiners so you can build a tended friction hitch system in one purchase. The hitch climber pulley keeps your hitch dressed and lets you pull slack through smoothly as you climb.
highlights: Built around the DMM Hitch Climber eccentric pulley
Matched connectors sized to fit the pulley's attachment holes
Tends slack through the hitch as you advance
Keeps the hitch cord's eyes separated and organized
A simple starting point for a pulley-tended friction hitch
specs: Two for hitch cord eyes, one for the bridge

body.h: Why climbers use a hitch climber setup
p: A friction hitch on its own works, but it needs a hand to tend it. With a hitch climber pulley under the hitch, you can pull slack through the pulley as you advance, and the hitch follows along without you holding it. The pulley also keeps the two eyes of your hitch cord apart, which helps the hitch release and reset consistently.
Buying the kit saves you from matching connectors yourself. The carabiners are chosen to fit the pulley's holes and to sit in the right orientation.

Matched connectors also help with inspection, because you are always checking the same parts in the same positions. That consistency matters when you build your system quickly at the base of the tree every morning.

Tie the hitch with a cord suited to your rope diameter, clip the eyes to the upper holes, and connect the lower hole to your bridge per DMM's instructions. Test the system low to the ground and make sure the hitch grabs when you let go. Add an eye-and-eye cord from our eye-and-eye prusiks range if you need one.
Anything you hang your life on must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and be inspected before every climb by a trained user.

If you already own a Hitch Climber pulley, you may only need the carabiners. Check the kit contents against your existing gear before buying, and replace any connector that shows wear, grooving or a sticky gate.

faq.q: Does the kit include a hitch cord?
faq.a: Check the listing for the specific kit you buy. Many climbers buy the cord separately so they can match diameter and material to their climb line.

faq.q: Is the Hitch Climber good for beginners?
faq.a: It is one of the most common ways to learn a tended friction hitch. Learn it from a qualified trainer and test it on the ground first.

name: Yale 8mm Beeline Hand-Spliced Eye-to-Eye
title: Yale 8mm Beeline Eye-to-Eye Hitch Cord, Hand Spliced
meta: The Yale 8mm Beeline eye-to-eye is a hand-spliced hitch cord for friction hitches like the Distel and VT. Rope pairing, care and typical street price.
tagline: An 8mm hand-spliced eye-to-eye hitch cord for consistent grab and release.
summary: The Yale 8mm Beeline eye-to-eye is a hitch cord with hand-spliced eyes on both ends, made for tying friction hitches on an arborist climbing line. Beeline is known for heat resistance and a firm hand that holds its shape in a hitch.
highlights: 8mm diameter suits many common arborist climbing lines
Hand-spliced eyes on both ends, no bulky knots
Heat-resistant cover helps on long or fast descents
Firm construction that holds a dressed hitch
Ready to use with a hitch-tending pulley

p: Spliced eyes are cleaner and more compact than tied knots, and they clip neatly to a hitch-tending pulley or carabiner. An 8mm cord is a common choice for 11 to 13 mm climbing lines, but the right pairing depends on both ropes, so test it before you trust it.
Beeline's cover is built to deal with the heat a friction hitch generates. That helps the cord stay consistent through a long day of descents.

Spliced cords also tend to be more consistent from one cord to the next, so if you replace a worn cord with the same product, the hitch should behave the same way. That makes it easier to keep a known, tested system on the saddle day after day.

Choose a length that suits the hitch you tie and how many wraps you need. Tie it, load it on the ground and adjust wraps until it grabs firmly and releases smoothly. Pair it with a pulley such as the DMM Hitch Climber.

Hitch cords wear faster than climbing lines. Retire the cord at signs of glazing, stiffness, cut fibers or a damaged splice. Anything you hang your life on must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and be inspected before every climb by a trained user.
Store spare cords in a clean bag away from fuel and chemicals, and do not mix cords of different diameters or materials without retesting your hitch.

faq.q: Will 8mm Beeline work on my climbing line?
faq.a: It works on many common arborist lines, but grab depends on both ropes. Always test the combination on the ground before climbing.

faq.q: How often should I replace a hitch cord?
faq.a: Inspect it before every climb and replace it at the first sign of glazing, stiffness, cuts or splice damage. Heavy users replace hitch cords often.

name: Yale 8mm Bee Line Split Tail
title: Yale 8mm Bee Line Split Tail for Friction Hitches
meta: The Yale 8mm Bee Line split tail is a heat-resistant hitch cord for tying friction hitches on your climb line. Lengths, rope pairing and typical price.
tagline: A heat-resistant 8mm split tail for climbers who tie their own friction hitch.
summary: The Yale 8mm Bee Line split tail is a length of hitch cord made for tying a friction hitch to your climbing line. A split tail separates the hitch from the end of your climb line, so you can replace the hitch cord without cutting the rope.
highlights: 8mm Bee Line cord with a heat-resistant cover
Firm hand that holds a dressed hitch
Lets you replace the hitch cord, not the rope
Works with Distel, VT and other common hitches

p: Before split tails, many climbers tied the hitch with the tail of their climb line. Heat and wear from the hitch then chewed up the end of the rope. A split tail moves that wear onto a separate, cheaper piece of cord that you can swap out on its own.
Bee Line is a good split tail material because it handles friction heat well and keeps its shape. Pair it with a pulley or tending device to make advancing easier.

The split tail is also cheap insurance for your climb line. Replacing a worn hitch cord costs a fraction of a new climbing rope, and it means the end of your line stays clean and strong for knots and terminations.
Inspect it before every climb for glazing, stiffness and cut fibers.

Tie terminations as taught by your trainer or use a pre-sewn or spliced version, and match the cord to your climb line. Test the hitch close to the ground and adjust wraps until it grabs and releases cleanly. Compare with spliced cords in our eye-and-eye prusiks section.
Anything you hang your life on must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and be inspected before every climb by a trained user.

Keep a spare split tail in your kit. Hitch cords wear quickly on long descents and in sandy or gritty conditions, and having a replacement ready means you can swap it at the tree instead of driving back to the shop.

faq.q: Is it spelled split tail or split tale?
faq.a: It is split tail, named for the tail of cord split off from the climbing line to tie the hitch.

faq.q: What length split tail do I need?
faq.a: That depends on the hitch and your terminations. Many climbers buy a little longer than needed and trim to length after testing on the ground.

name: MRS Climbing Devices
title: MRS Climbing Kit and Moving Rope Friction Devices
meta: Build an MRS climbing kit around a mechanical friction device for moving rope work. How MRS devices compare with hitches, what to pair them with and prices.
tagline: Mechanical friction devices for moving rope climbing, and how to build a kit around them.
summary: An MRS climbing kit built around a mechanical friction device replaces or supplements the traditional friction hitch for moving rope work. These devices give consistent grab and release on a doubled line, with less cord to maintain and less heat build-up on long descents.
highlights: Consistent grab and release on a doubled moving rope
Less cord wear and heat glazing than a pure friction hitch
Many devices also convert for stationary rope use
Fine control for limb walks and controlled descents
Pairs with a pulley, swivel and quality connectors for a complete kit
specs: Device, connectors, pulley or swivel, climb line
Check each device's rated diameter range

p: In moving rope climbing, your line runs from your saddle, up over an anchor and back down to your friction system. The climber advances by pulling slack through the system. For decades that meant a friction hitch and a hitch-tending pulley. Mechanical MRS devices do the same job with metal parts that grip the rope through a cam, chain or bend path.

The appeal is consistency. A hitch can grab differently when cord is new, worn, wet or hot. A mechanical device behaves the same from the first climb of the morning to the last, as long as it is used on a compatible rope and kept clean.
Mechanical devices also reduce the heat that builds up on long descents, which helps protect your climbing line and gives you smoother control when you are lowering yourself out of a big tree.

Start with the device and check its approved rope diameters and rope types against your climb line. Then add connectors the manufacturer approves, a small pulley or swivel if the device is designed for one, and a friction saver or ring set for the anchor. Rings from our rings section are a common choice.
Many climbers keep a friction hitch setup as a backup and for rescue scenarios. Knowing both systems makes you a more flexible climber.

If you plan to move between moving and stationary rope, look for a device that is approved for both. Converting between modes usually means adding or rearranging components, and the steps must follow the manual exactly.
Write down what you build and keep it the same. A consistent setup is easier to inspect and easier for a crew partner to check during a buddy check or a rescue.

Think about how you climb most. Long limb walks and big spreading trees reward a device with very fine descent control. Fast production climbing on smaller trees rewards something quick to install and easy to tend. Weight, how easily the device releases with gloves on, and how well it handles a dirty rope all matter on a real job.
Ask other climbers on your crew what they run, and try a device before you buy if you can. For stationary rope options, see our SRS climbing devices page.
Price matters too. A good MRS device is a real investment, so it pays to choose one that fits your rope, your trees and your style rather than chasing the newest design.

Mechanical devices change how your system behaves under load, and misrigging can be serious. Learn a new device from a qualified trainer, rig it on the ground, and test it before every climb. Keep it clean of sap and grit, check moving parts for wear, and retire it if anything is cracked, bent or worn past the maker's limits.
Anything you hang your life on must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and be inspected before every climb by a trained user.
Keep the device's manual with your kit or saved on your phone, and recheck it whenever you change rope or connectors.

faq.q: Is a mechanical MRS device better than a friction hitch?
faq.a: It is more consistent and needs less cord maintenance, but it costs more and has its own learning curve. Many climbers carry both.

faq.q: Can MRS devices be used for SRS?
faq.a: Some devices are approved for both systems with the right setup. Check the manufacturer's instructions for the specific device.

faq.q: What rope works with an MRS device?
faq.a: Each device lists approved rope diameters and constructions. Using a rope outside that range can affect grab and control.

name: SRS Climbing Devices
title: SRS Climbing Devices and Mechanical Prusik Options
meta: Compare SRS climbing devices, from mechanical prusik units to rope wrench setups, for stationary rope tree work. What to look for and typical prices.
tagline: Descent and work-positioning devices for stationary rope technique.
summary: SRS climbing devices, often called a mechanical prusik when they replace a friction hitch, control your descent and positioning on a single stationary line. They let a climber ascend efficiently and work the canopy on one rope anchored at the base or high in the tree.
highlights: Controlled descent and positioning on a single stationary line
Efficient ascent when paired with ascenders and a foot loop
Consistent friction compared with a hitch alone
Options for different rope diameters and climbing styles
specs: Check each device's rated diameter range

body.h: How SRS devices fit into a system
p: On a stationary rope the line does not move through the anchor; you move along it. That means your device does all the friction work, and it needs to give smooth control without excessive heat. Some setups use a friction hitch tended by a device, others use a fully mechanical unit. Ascent is handled with chest and foot ascenders or a rope-walking setup.
A good SRS kit also includes a base anchor or retrievable canopy anchor, quality connectors and a rope within the device's rated range. See moving-rope options on our MRS climbing devices page.

Stationary rope work also changes how you think about anchors. The anchor carries the full load on a single line, and a canopy anchor sees forces differently than a moving rope redirect. Choosing the anchor point and tie-off method is as important as choosing the device.

Look at rope compatibility, how the device handles a long descent, how easy it is to lock off for work positioning and how it behaves with gloves on. Learn SRS from a qualified trainer; anchoring and rescue are different from moving rope work.
Anything you hang your life on must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and be inspected before every climb by a trained user.
Many climbers keep both MRS and SRS gear in the truck and pick the system that suits each tree. Learning both makes you more flexible, and it gives you options for rescue.

faq.q: What is a mechanical prusik?
faq.a: It is a mechanical device that does the job of a friction hitch, grabbing the rope under load and releasing for descent or advancing.

faq.q: Do I need different rope for SRS?
faq.a: Many arborist climbing lines work for SRS, but each device has an approved diameter and construction range. Match your rope to the device.

name: CMI Micro Rescue Pulley
title: CMI Micro Rescue Pulley: Compact Pulley for Tree Work
meta: The CMI micro rescue pulley is a compact, high-strength pulley for hitch tending, mechanical advantage and rescue setups. Uses, specs and typical price.
tagline: A small, strong pulley for hitch tending, haul systems and rescue kits.
summary: The CMI micro rescue pulley is a compact pulley that earns a spot on a lot of climbing saddles. It tends a friction hitch, builds small mechanical advantage systems and goes into a rescue kit without adding much weight.
highlights: Compact enough to ride on the saddle all day
Useful for hitch tending, haul systems and rescue
Rated as a rescue pulley by CMI
Light enough to carry a spare in a rescue kit

p: A micro pulley is one of the most useful bits of hardware on a saddle. Under a friction hitch it lets you pull slack through with one hand. On the ground it turns a rigging line into a simple 3:1 for tensioning or pulling a leaner. In a rescue kit it helps build a lowering or raising system in a hurry.

Because it is small, a micro pulley is easy to carry as a spare. Many climbers keep one on the saddle for the hitch and a second in a rescue kit or rigging bag, so a mechanical advantage system is always within reach when a piece hangs up or a climber needs help.
Retire it if the sheave wobbles, the bushing is worn or the side plates are bent.

Confirm the pulley suits your rope diameter, use locking connectors, and follow CMI's instructions for loading. Keep the sheave clean of sap and grit and check that it spins freely. See more options in our micro pulleys section.
Anything you hang your life on must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and be inspected before every climb by a trained user.
Before you buy, check that the pulley fits your connectors and rope. A sheave that is too narrow can bind, and a connector that does not sit right can cross-load.

faq.q: Can I use it to tend a friction hitch?
faq.a: Yes. Many climbers run a micro pulley under their hitch. Check that it fits your hitch cord and connectors and test the setup on the ground.

faq.q: What rope size does it take?
faq.a: It is built for common arborist and rescue rope sizes. Check the markings and CMI's instructions for the exact range.

name: DMM Hitch Climber Eccentric Pulley
title: DMM Hitch Climber Pulley: Eccentric Hitch Tender
meta: The DMM Hitch Climber pulley tends your friction hitch and keeps the cord dressed as you advance. How the eccentric design works, setup and typical price.
tagline: The hitch-tending pulley many tree climbers build their friction hitch around.
summary: The DMM Hitch Climber pulley is an eccentric hitch-tending pulley that sits under your friction hitch and lets you pull slack through smoothly. Its offset attachment points keep the hitch cord eyes apart and the bridge connection in line, so the hitch stays dressed and releases cleanly.
highlights: Eccentric design keeps hitch eyes and bridge connection organized
Two upper holes for hitch cord eyes, one lower hole for the bridge
Smooth slack tending as you advance
Available in different colors for system identification

p: A plain pulley under a hitch works, but the hitch cord eyes and the bridge connector tend to fight for space. The Hitch Climber gives each its own hole, with the upper holes for the eyes of your hitch cord and the lower hole for the connector to your bridge. That keeps the hitch tied the same way every time and makes it easier to break and reset.
Pull the tail of your climb line through the sheave as you go up and the hitch follows along without you holding it.

Many climbers keep the same pulley on their system for years, replacing the hitch cord around it as it wears. That makes the Hitch Climber a good long-term investment, as long as you inspect it and keep the sheave clean.
Inspect the sheave, bushing and holes for wear and grooving, and retire the pulley if it is damaged.

Use connectors that fit the holes and sit in the right orientation; the DMM Hitch Climber Kit pairs the pulley with matched carabiners. Match your hitch cord to your climb line and test on the ground.
Anything you hang your life on must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and be inspected before every climb by a trained user.
The color options are also useful on crews where several climbers share a truck. Each climber can run their own color, so systems do not get mixed up at the end of the day.

faq.q: What carabiners work with the Hitch Climber?
faq.a: Use locking connectors that fit the holes without cross-loading. DMM sells a kit with matched carabiners if you want a ready-made set.

faq.q: Can I use the Hitch Climber for SRS?
faq.a: It is mostly used for moving rope friction hitches. Some SRS setups use it as part of the system, but follow the manufacturer's guidance.

name: DMM Captain Hook
title: DMM Captain Hook: Gear Hook for Climbing Saddles
meta: The DMM Captain Hook is a quick-clip hook for hanging tools and gear from your saddle or a branch. What it is for, what it is not for and typical price.
tagline: A quick-clip accessory hook for keeping tools and gear within reach aloft.
summary: The DMM Captain Hook is an accessory hook that keeps tools and gear handy while you work aloft. Clip it to your saddle or a branch to hang a hand saw, a rope bag or extra hardware where you can grab it.
highlights: Quick to clip and unclip with gloves on
Keeps tools and gear off your harness connectors
Light enough to carry a couple on the saddle
Not for life support

p: Every climber runs out of room on the saddle at some point. A dedicated gear hook gives your hand saw, spare carabiners or a small rope bag a place to hang so they are not cluttering your life-support connectors. Clip it to a gear loop or a sturdy branch and your tools stay where you can reach them.
That matters on long removals and big prunes, where you move between tools often and do not want to fumble at the side D-rings.

Hooks like this are especially handy when you are switching between a handsaw and a top-handle saw, or carrying a throw line and small rope bag up for a redirect. Instead of clipping everything to whatever connector is free, you give each item a place.
Keep them light. If you are hanging something heavy enough to worry about, it belongs on a rated attachment designed for that load.

Accessory hooks are for carrying gear, not people. Never clip it into your climbing system, lanyard or rigging. Keep life-support connectors and accessory hooks visually distinct so nobody mixes them up. Browse related hardware in other climbing gear.
Check it regularly for bends and gate damage, and replace it if it no longer closes cleanly.
Mark accessory hooks clearly, for example with colored tape, so they are never confused with rated carabiners in a hurry. That small habit prevents a dangerous mistake.

faq.q: Can I use the Captain Hook as a carabiner?
faq.a: No. Treat it as an accessory for hanging gear. Use rated locking connectors for anything in your climbing or rigging system.

faq.q: What can I hang on it?
faq.a: Hand saws, small rope bags, spare hardware and similar light gear. Keep chainsaws on a dedicated saw lanyard or saw strap.

name: The SawPod
title: The SawPod: Chainsaw Holder for Climbing Arborists
meta: The SawPod gives a climbing arborist a secure place to park a top-handle saw aloft instead of letting it dangle. How it works, who it suits and typical price.
tagline: A purpose-built place to park your saw aloft so it is not swinging off your saddle.
summary: The SawPod is a chainsaw holder for climbing arborists that gives a top-handle saw a secure place to sit while you work aloft. Instead of letting the saw hang off a lanyard and bang against your legs, you set it in the SawPod and pick it back up when you are ready to cut.
highlights: Parks a top-handle saw securely while you reposition or rig
Keeps the saw from swinging against your legs and lanyard
Reduces wear and snag risk on your saw lanyard and climbing system
Frees both hands for tying off pieces and setting anchors
Simple to set and retrieve the saw with gloves on
specs: Top-handle chainsaws (check fit for your model)
Saw storage aloft, not life support

p: Every climber who runs a top-handle saw knows the routine. You make your cut, shut the saw off or set the brake, and let it drop onto the saw lanyard. Then it swings. It bumps your thigh, it twists your lanyard, it hangs in the way of your climbing line and it catches on branches when you move. On a big removal you might do that a hundred times in a day.

The SawPod gives the saw a home. Set the saw in it while you tie off the next piece, re-anchor or move across the canopy, then pick it back up when you are ready to cut. The saw stays still, your hands are free, and the bar is not swinging near your rope.

On a big removal, you might set the saw down and pick it up dozens of times an hour. Cutting out a little swinging each time adds up to less fatigue and less wear on your lanyard and clothing by the end of the day.

Most use it when they need both hands for a while: tying a rigging knot, setting a redirect, limb walking or working a pole saw. It is also useful when you are dealing with a hung piece and want the saw parked somewhere predictable rather than hanging below you.

Keep your saw lanyard connected at all times. The SawPod is a convenience for where the saw sits, not a replacement for a proper saw lanyard or saw strap. Set the chain brake every time you park the saw, and never park a running saw unless the manufacturer and your company's procedures allow it.
It also helps when you have to talk to the ground crew. Parking the saw means you are not holding it while you signal or adjust a rigging line.

Top-handle saws are made for use aloft by trained arborists. If you are building out your climbing saw kit, consider the whole system: the saw, a saw lanyard with a breakaway or swivel, a scabbard for the bar, and a place to park it. Browse other aloft accessories in other climbing gear.
Check that the SawPod fits your saw's handle and that it sits where you can reach it without twisting. A little practice on the ground makes the motion automatic.
Think about where it sits on your setup. A position that is easy to reach without looking makes the habit stick, and that is what makes the tool worth carrying.

Follow ANSI Z133 for chainsaw use aloft, including one-handed operation limits, and only run a top-handle saw if you are trained to do so. Keep the SawPod clean of chips and bar oil and check it for cracks or wear where the saw sits. Replace it if it no longer holds the saw securely.
Because it is not part of your climbing system, never clip it into life-support gear or use it as an anchor.
If it gets damaged, replace it rather than repairing it with tape or wire, which can catch the chain.

faq.q: Does the SawPod replace a saw lanyard?
faq.a: No. Keep your saw lanyard attached whenever the saw is aloft. The SawPod just gives the saw a stable place to sit.

faq.q: Will it fit my top-handle saw?
faq.a: It is designed for common top-handle saws. Check the maker's fit notes for your model before buying.

faq.q: Can ground workers use it?
faq.a: It is designed for climbers working aloft. On the ground, a proper saw case or scabbard is the better storage option.

name: DMM Anchor Rings
title: DMM Anchor Rings for Friction Savers and Rigging
meta: DMM anchor rings are forged rings for building friction savers, adjustable anchors and light rigging. Sizes, materials, uses and typical price explained.
tagline: Strong, smooth rings for building climbing anchors and friction savers.
summary: DMM anchor rings are forged rings used to build friction savers, adjustable anchors and simple rigging connections. Their smooth bore lets rope run over them with low friction, which is why so many climbers build ring-and-ring savers around DMM anchor rings.
highlights: Smooth, rounded bore that is easy on rope
Used for ring-and-ring friction savers and cambium savers
Common building block for adjustable canopy anchors
Available in different sizes and materials
Simple to inspect, with no moving parts

body.h: Why rings are everywhere in tree climbing
p: A ring is the simplest piece of hardware you can own. No gate, no sleeve, no moving parts. That makes it ideal at the top of a climbing system, where the rope runs back and forth through the anchor and you want as little friction and wear as possible.

A ring-and-ring friction saver is the classic example: a sling with a large ring on one end and a small ring on the other. You install it around a union, run your line through both rings, and the rope runs over smooth metal instead of bark. When you are done, the small ring passes through the large one so you can retrieve the saver from the ground.

Rings also work well as the bottom connection on a basal anchor for stationary rope, or as a gathering point for a multi-sling anchor where you want everything to sit together without cross-loading a connector.

body.h: Ring sizes and why they matter
p: Ring size affects what can pass through it and how rope bends over it. On a retrievable friction saver, the small ring has to pass through the large one, so the pair must be sized to work together. A larger ring gives a gentler bend radius and smoother running.

Rings come in aluminum and steel versions. Aluminum is lighter and fine for most climbing anchors. Steel stands up better to abrasion and is often chosen for heavy-use applications. Check DMM's rated strength for the exact ring you buy and keep within it.
Buy rings in matched pairs if you are building retrievable savers, and keep a spare pair in your kit for when a saver gets stuck or damaged.

Rings pair with eye-to-eye slings, adjustable cambium savers and spliced loops. You can also use them as a clean connection point for a lanyard or as part of a simple redirect. Compare options with the Petzl Ring Open, which can be opened and closed around a sling or rope.
Do not mix climbing anchors and rigging loads without understanding the forces. Rigging can generate loads well beyond what a climbing anchor sees.
For climbers who do not want to build their own, many pre-made ring savers use DMM rings. If you build your own, follow manufacturer guidance and get the construction checked by a qualified person.

Inspect rings for grooving where rope runs, sharp edges, cracks and deformation. Aluminum rings wear faster when gritty rope runs over them, so keep your line clean. Retire a ring if wear is visible or if it has taken a major shock load.
Anything you hang your life on must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and be inspected before every climb by a trained user.
Keep a simple record of when you started using each ring, and retire rings that see heavy rope traffic before wear becomes deep.

faq.q: Can I use DMM anchor rings to make a friction saver?
faq.a: Yes. Ring-and-ring friction savers are one of their most common uses. Size the rings so the small one passes through the large one.

faq.q: Aluminum or steel?
faq.a: Aluminum is lighter and common for climbing anchors. Steel resists abrasion better for heavy use. Check the rating of the ring you choose.

faq.q: Can rings be used for rigging?
faq.a: Rings can be part of light rigging setups, but rigging loads can be high. Stay within the rated strength and get trained in rigging forces.

name: Petzl Ring Open
title: Petzl Ring Open: Openable Anchor Ring for Climbers
meta: The Petzl Ring Open is an openable anchor ring you can install around a sling, rope or anchor without threading. Uses, care and typical price inside.
tagline: An openable ring that installs around slings and anchors without threading an end.
summary: The Petzl Ring Open is an anchor ring that opens, so you can add it to a sling, rope or anchor without threading anything through. Climbers use the Petzl open ring to build anchors, attach to existing slings and set up multi-point connections.
highlights: Opens to install around slings, rope eyes and anchors
Smooth rounded bore that is easy on textiles
Useful for multi-point anchors and quick connections
Closes securely for use as a connection ring

p: A closed ring has to be installed before the sling is sewn or the rope is spliced. The Ring Open removes that limit. Open it, place it around the sling, eye or anchor, close it, and you have a smooth connection point in seconds.
That is handy when building anchors that connect several slings, when adding a ring to an existing cambium saver, or when you want a clean attachment point on a saddle bridge or rigging setup.
It is also handy as a spare in a rescue kit. If you need to add a connection point to a sling or anchor quickly, an openable ring is faster than rebuilding the anchor.
Keep the opening mechanism clean; sap and grit can make it hard to close fully.

Make sure the ring is fully closed and secured per Petzl's instructions every time you load it. Inspect the opening mechanism, bore and body for wear, cracks and grit. Compare with closed rings like the Petzl Ring.
Anything you hang your life on must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and be inspected before every climb by a trained user.
Train yourself to check closure every time, the same way you check a carabiner gate. Make the check part of your routine so it happens even when you are in a hurry.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Petzl Ring and Ring Open?
faq.a: The standard Ring is a closed ring. The Ring Open has an opening so it can be installed around slings and anchors without threading.

faq.q: Can I use it in a climbing anchor?
faq.a: Yes, when it is closed and secured according to Petzl's instructions and used within its rating. Check it before every climb.

name: Petzl Ring
title: Petzl Ring: Aluminum Anchor Ring for Tree Climbing
meta: The Petzl Ring is a light aluminum ring for building friction savers, anchors and multi-point connections. Sizes, how arborists use it and typical price.
tagline: A light, smooth aluminum ring for friction savers and anchor building.
summary: The Petzl Ring is a closed aluminum ring that climbers use to build friction savers, anchors and multi-point connections. It is simple, light and smooth on rope, which makes the Petzl ring a staple in a lot of climbing kits.
highlights: Light aluminum ring with a smooth bore
Available in small and large sizes
Builds ring-and-ring friction savers and anchors
No moving parts to wear out

body.h: Where it fits in your kit
p: Rings are the cleanest way to give your rope a smooth path at the anchor. Pair a small and a large Petzl Ring on a sling and you have a retrievable friction saver. Use one on a multi-point anchor to gather several slings into a single connection.
Because it is closed, it is installed when the sling or eye is built. If you need to add a ring to an existing sling, look at the Petzl Ring Open.
Because the Petzl Ring is so light, it is easy to carry a spare pair. If a saver gets stuck or damaged in the canopy, having replacements in the truck saves a trip to the shop.
Retire rings that have been dropped onto rock or concrete if you see dents or cracks.
Keep rope clean so grit does not groove the aluminum. Inspect for wear, sharp edges and cracks, and retire the ring if you see any.
Anything you hang your life on must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and be inspected before every climb by a trained user.

Small and large rings are also handy when building adjustable anchors and simple multi-point setups. Keep spare rings separate from rigging hardware so they are not used for heavy loads beyond their rating.

faq.q: Which size should I buy?
faq.a: For a retrievable friction saver you need a small ring that passes through a large one. Check sizing before you build.

faq.q: Is the Petzl Ring strong enough for climbing?
faq.a: It is made as a connection ring for climbing systems. Use it within Petzl's rating and instructions and inspect it before every climb.

name: CMI California Swivel
title: CMI Gear California Swivel for Climbing and Rigging
meta: The CMI California Swivel is a compact swivel from CMI Gear that takes twist out of climbing systems and light rigging. How it is used and typical price.
tagline: A compact CMI swivel that keeps rope and lanyards from twisting.
summary: The CMI California Swivel is a compact swivel from CMI Gear that keeps rope, lanyards and loads from twisting. Placed between connectors, it lets the system rotate freely so your line hangs clean.
highlights: Free rotation that takes twist out of rope systems
Compact size that sits neatly between connectors
Used in climbing systems and light rigging
Made by CMI, a long-time rescue and rope access hardware maker

p: Rope twists. Every time you spin while descending, or a load rotates on the way down, twist builds into the line. A swivel lets one side of the system turn without the other, so your climb line stays cleaner and your friction system works the way it should.
Climbers often put a swivel between a friction device and the saddle bridge. In light rigging, a swivel between a block and a load stops a spinning piece from winding the rope.

Swivels also help when you are working with long lanyards or a rope that has picked up twist from a previous job. A swivel in the right place lets that twist run out instead of kinking at your device.
Check compatibility with your device and connectors before buying. A swivel that is too long can change how your system sits on the bridge.

Use rated locking connectors at each end, follow CMI's rating and instructions, and check that the swivel turns smoothly under light load. Retire it if rotation is rough or the body is damaged. See more in our swivels section.
Anything you hang your life on must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and be inspected before every climb by a trained user.
Keep the swivel clean, since grit in the bearing makes rotation rough and can hide wear. Rinse it with clean water if it gets dirty and let it dry fully before storage.

faq.q: Where should I put a swivel in my climbing system?
faq.a: A common spot is between the friction device and the bridge. Follow the device maker's guidance and test on the ground.

faq.q: Can it be used for rigging?
faq.a: It can be part of light rigging within its rating. Rigging loads can be high, so understand the forces before using it.

name: Petzl Micro Swivel Open
title: Petzl Micro Swivel Open: Compact Openable Swivel
meta: The Petzl Micro Swivel Open is a compact swivel that opens to install directly on a bridge or sling. How it fits arborist climbing systems and typical price.
tagline: A small, openable swivel that installs directly on a saddle bridge or sling.
summary: The Petzl Micro Swivel Open is a compact swivel with an openable side, so it can be installed directly on a saddle bridge, sling or rope eye. Like the standard Petzl micro swivel, it keeps your system from twisting while adding very little bulk.
highlights: Openable side for direct installation on bridges and slings
Compact, low-profile swivel
Keeps friction devices aligned and rope untwisted
Saves a connector compared with a closed swivel

p: A closed swivel needs a connector on each side. The Open version can be installed directly on a bridge or sling, which cuts out a connector, lowers the profile and keeps your friction device closer to the saddle. Many climbers use it to hang an SRS device or friction system from the bridge so it can rotate freely.
Fewer connectors also means fewer things to cross-load.

The low profile also helps when you are working close to the bridge or using an SRS device that needs to sit a certain distance from the saddle. Fewer parts between you and the device means less length and a more direct feel.
Keep it clean and rinse it if it gets gritty. Rough rotation is a sign it needs attention or replacement.

Make sure the opening is fully closed and secured per Petzl's instructions before loading. Inspect the swivel for smooth rotation and check the opening mechanism for wear and grit. Compare with the CMI California Swivel.
Anything you hang your life on must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and be inspected before every climb by a trained user.
Swivels make rope twist less of a problem, but they do not fix bad technique. Avoid spinning on long descents, and take twist out of your rope by letting it hang free when you can.

faq.q: Can I install it directly on my saddle bridge?
faq.a: That is what the openable side is for. Follow Petzl's instructions and check compatibility with your bridge.

faq.q: What is the difference from the regular Micro Swivel?
faq.a: The regular version is closed and needs connectors on both ends. The Open version can be installed directly on a sling or bridge.

name: Husqvarna Technical Forestry Helmet
title: Husqvarna Helmet: Technical Forestry Helmet System
meta: This Husqvarna helmet system pairs a forestry hard hat with a mesh visor and earmuffs for saw work. Features, fit, who it suits and typical price inside.
tagline: A forestry helmet system with visor and earmuffs for felling, bucking and ground saw work.
summary: The Husqvarna Technical forestry helmet is a Husqvarna helmet system that pairs a hard hat with a mesh visor and earmuffs, so head, face and hearing protection go on in one piece. It is built for chainsaw work on the ground: felling, bucking, limbing and clearing.
highlights: Hard hat, mesh visor and earmuffs in one system
Adjustable headband for a secure fit
Ventilated shell for hot days on the saw
Visor and muffs flip up when you are off the saw
Replaceable components for long service

body.h: One hard hat for the whole saw job
p: Running a chainsaw means dealing with three hazards at once: things falling on your head, chips flying at your face and noise loud enough to damage hearing over time. A forestry helmet system handles all three, so you are not juggling a hard hat, safety glasses and a separate set of muffs.

The Husqvarna Technical is aimed at ground saw work. Felling, bucking logs, limbing brush and clearing lots are where it fits best. The mesh visor stops chips and small debris while letting air through, and the earmuffs attach to the helmet so they sit at the right pressure every time you put it on.
That makes it a good fit for crews that do a lot of land clearing, storm cleanup and firewood work, where people spend hours running a saw at ground level.

A helmet you do not wear does not protect you, so comfort matters. The adjustable headband lets you snug the fit before you start the saw and loosen it when you take a break. Vents in the shell help on hot days, and the visor and muffs flip up when you step off the saw to drag brush or talk to the crew.

Many saw operators still wear safety glasses under the mesh visor. A mesh screen stops chips but not fine dust or splinters at every angle. Add glasses from our safety gear range for full eye protection.
Check the seal of the earmuffs against your head with the helmet on. Glasses frames and hair can break the seal, and that lets in more noise than you think.

Forestry helmets like this are classic ground worker hard hats. Climbers usually prefer a dedicated climbing helmet with a chin strap that keeps the helmet on during a fall or swing, such as the Petzl Vertex Vent or Kask Super Plasma. Check what your employer requires for each role on the crew.
If you are a homeowner or part-time saw user, a Husqvarna hard hat system like this is one of the simplest ways to cover the basics in one purchase.
A Husqvarna hard hat system also works well for crew members who split time between the saw, the chipper and dragging brush, since the visor and muffs move out of the way quickly.

Keep the helmet out of direct sun in the truck cab when you can, wipe off bar oil and sap, and check the shell for cracks and the suspension for wear. Replace the earmuff cushions when they flatten or crack, since a poor seal lets noise in.

Choose a helmet that meets the standard your employer and ANSI Z133 require for the work you do, fit it per the manufacturer's instructions, and replace it after a significant impact or when it reaches the maker's service life.
Write the date you started using the helmet inside the shell so you know when to replace it.

faq.q: Is the Husqvarna Technical helmet good for climbing?
faq.a: It is designed mainly for ground saw work. Climbers usually choose a climbing-style helmet with a secure chin strap. Check your employer's requirements.

faq.q: Do I still need safety glasses?
faq.a: Many operators wear safety glasses under the mesh visor for better protection from fine dust and splinters.

faq.q: Can I replace the visor and earmuffs?
faq.a: Husqvarna sells replacement parts for its helmet systems. Check that parts match your helmet model.

name: Kask Super Plasma Climbing Helmet
title: Kask Super Plasma Helmet for Arborists and Climbers
meta: The Kask Super Plasma is a vented arborist helmet built for climbing and aerial work. Fit, accessories, how it compares and typical street price inside.
tagline: A popular climbing helmet for arborists who want comfort, airflow and accessory options.
summary: The Kask Super Plasma is a climbing helmet that has become a common sight in tree crews thanks to its comfort, airflow and accessory options. The Super Plasma helmet is built for climbing and aerial work, with a secure chin strap and slots for visors and hearing protection.
highlights: Ventilated shell for long days aloft
Secure chin strap for climbing and aerial work
Wheel adjustment for a quick, precise fit
Accepts Kask visors and hearing protection
Washable, replaceable padding
Available in several colors including high-visibility options

body.h: Why so many climbers wear it
p: A climbing helmet spends eight hours a day on your head, so small differences in comfort add up. The Super Plasma is light on the head, well vented and easy to adjust, and the padding can be pulled out and washed after a sweaty week. For many climbers it is the helmet they forget they are wearing, which is exactly what you want.
The chin strap keeps the helmet on during a slip, swing or fall, which is the main difference between a climbing helmet and a traditional hard hat. A hard hat can come off when you need it most.
Many climbers also like that the shell shape and color options make the helmet easy to spot from the ground, which helps when the ground crew is watching a climber work high in the canopy.

The Super Plasma is also a common choice for bucket work, where a chin strap keeps the helmet on if you lean out of the basket or catch a branch. Kask arborist helmet versions with closed shells are the ones to check for electrical work, while vented versions suit climbing in hot weather.

body.h: Accessories that turn it into a system
p: The Super Plasma takes Kask's range of visors and earmuffs, so you can set it up for climbing with a saw. A mesh or clear visor protects your face from chips and twigs, and helmet-mounted muffs drop over your ears when you start the saw and flip up when you are rigging or talking to the ground crew.
If you run a radio headset, check compatibility before you buy, because mounting systems differ between brands.
If you run a headlamp for early starts or storm work, the accessory clips make it simple to mount one securely.

body.h: Kask arborist helmet or something else
p: Climbers often compare the Super Plasma with the Petzl Vertex Vent and the Pfanner Protos Integral. The Vertex Vent has a different suspension feel, while the Protos is a fully integrated system with built-in hearing and face protection. Try them on if you can, since head shape matters more than any spec sheet.

There are several versions of the Super Plasma, including vented and unvented and high-visibility models. Check the exact version and its certifications against what your employer requires, especially for utility line clearance work where electrical ratings matter.
Weight and balance matter too. Once you add a visor and muffs, the total load on your neck goes up, so try the full setup on before you commit, not just the bare helmet.
Wash the pads, wipe the shell clean of sap and bar oil, and avoid solvents and stickers that the manufacturer does not approve. Inspect the shell, chin strap and adjustment system regularly.

Choose a helmet that meets the standard your employer and ANSI Z133 require for the work you do, fit it per the manufacturer's instructions, and replace it after a significant impact or when it reaches the maker's service life.
Replace the pads when they flatten or stop wicking, since worn pads change how the helmet sits.

faq.q: Is the Kask Super Plasma good for tree climbing?
faq.a: Yes. It is one of the most widely used arborist climbing helmets, with a chin strap, good ventilation and accessory mounts for visors and muffs.

faq.q: Can I use it for electrical line clearance?
faq.a: Only versions certified for electrical protection are suitable. Vented models are not. Check the label and your employer's requirements.

faq.q: Does it come with a visor and earmuffs?
faq.a: The helmet is usually sold on its own, with visors and earmuffs sold separately or in kits. Check the listing.

name: Petzl Vertex Vent Helmet
title: Petzl Vertex Vent: Petzl Helmet for Tree Climbers
meta: The Petzl Vertex Vent is a ventilated Petzl helmet built for climbing and work at height. Fit system, accessories, versions and typical price explained.
tagline: A ventilated work-at-height helmet with a secure fit for long days in the canopy.
summary: The Petzl Vertex Vent is a Petzl helmet built for climbing and work at height, with closable vents for airflow and a chin strap that keeps it on through slips and swings. Its textile suspension and adjustment system give a stable, comfortable fit for long days aloft.
highlights: Closable vents for airflow on hot days
Textile suspension for a comfortable, stable fit
Chin strap for climbing and work at height
Accessory slots for visors, earmuffs and headlamps
Weight of about 490 g

p: The Petzl Vertex has been a standard in rope access, rescue and tree work for a long time. The Vertex Vent is the ventilated version, with sliding shutters that let you open the vents on hot days and close them to keep out sawdust and rain. For climbers who work through the summer, that airflow makes a real difference.
Like all climbing helmets, it has a chin strap that keeps the helmet on during a slip, swing or fall. That is something a traditional hard hat does not do.
Many crews use the Vertex Vent as a standard climbing helmet for exactly that reason: it works in hot weather and still keeps out debris when the vents are closed.

For new climbers, the Vertex Vent is a sensible first helmet because it is widely used, easy to adjust and well supported with spare parts. Pads, chin straps and accessories are easy to find, which keeps the helmet in service longer.

The Vertex uses a textile suspension that cradles the head instead of perching on it. Combined with the adjustment system, it gives a stable fit that does not shift when you look up into the canopy or lean over a cut. Many climbers with longer heads find the Petzl vertex a better fit than rounder helmets, but head shape varies, so try it on if you can.
The pads are removable and washable, which helps over a long season.
Adjustment is quick, so you can snug the fit when you start climbing and loosen it on breaks. That makes it easier to wear the helmet all day instead of taking it off between climbs.
Petzl also publishes clear inspection guidance, so it is easy to build the helmet into your daily gear check along with your saddle and rope.

Slots on the shell accept Petzl visors, helmet-mounted earmuffs and headlamps, so you can build it into a full saw-ready setup. There are also high-visibility and unvented versions; unvented helmets are the option to look at when electrical insulation matters. Check the label on the exact model against your employer's requirements.
Climbers often compare it with the Kask Super Plasma. Both are excellent; fit usually decides it. Browse all options in our climbing helmets section.

When you add accessories, check that the combination is approved by Petzl. Mixing parts from different makers can affect fit and protection, and some accessories may not fit every version of the helmet.
Keep the helmet out of strong sun when stored, clean it with mild soap and water, and avoid solvents and unapproved stickers. Check the shell, suspension and chin strap for damage.

Choose a helmet that meets the standard your employer and ANSI Z133 require for the work you do, fit it per the manufacturer's instructions, and replace it after a significant impact or when it reaches the maker's service life.
Keep a note of when you started using it, and check the manufacturer's recommended service life for your version.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Vertex and the Vertex Vent?
faq.a: The Vertex Vent has closable ventilation openings. The non-vented Vertex is the choice when you need a closed shell, such as for some electrical work.

faq.q: Can I add earmuffs and a visor to the Petzl Vertex Vent?
faq.a: Yes. It has slots for Petzl-compatible earmuffs and visors, plus clips for a headlamp.

faq.q: How much does the Vertex Vent weigh?
faq.a: About 490 g, or roughly 17 ounces, before accessories.

name: Pfanner Protos Integral Arborist Helmet System
title: Protos Helmet: Pfanner Protos Integral Arborist System
h1: Pfanner Protos Integral Arborist Helmet System
meta: The Pfanner Protos helmet integrates hearing, face and head protection in one arborist system. How it fits, who it suits, versions and typical price inside.
tagline: A fully integrated arborist helmet with built-in hearing and face protection.
summary: The Pfanner Protos Integral Arborist is the Protos helmet built for climbers, with head, face and hearing protection designed together as one system rather than bolted on. Its chin strap, integrated earmuffs and visor make it a favorite for arborists who run a saw aloft all day.
highlights: Integrated earmuffs and visor designed into the helmet
Chin strap for climbing and work at height
Adjustable fit system for long days aloft
Ventilation for hot weather
Accessory options including neck protection and radio kits
Replaceable parts to extend service life

body.h: An integrated system, not a helmet with add-ons
p: Most helmets start as a shell, then you add a visor and earmuffs. The Protos was designed the other way around. The earmuffs and visor are part of the helmet's shape, which keeps everything balanced on your head and stops parts from snagging on branches. It has a distinctive look that has made the Protos helmet one of the most recognized pieces of arborist gear.
The Integral Arborist version adds a chin strap so the helmet stays on during a slip or swing, which is what separates a climbing helmet from a ground hard hat.

The integrated design also means fewer parts to lose or forget. When the helmet is on, you have your face and hearing protection with you, which is a big deal for climbers who move between cutting and rigging all day.

Comfort is a big reason climbers pay more for the Protos. When hearing protection, face protection and fit are designed together, the helmet feels balanced and stable, and many climbers say they forget they are wearing it after a few hours.

Climbers who run a top-handle saw all day tend to love the Protos. The muffs flip up and down quickly, and the visor drops into place without bumping the muffs. Ventilation helps on hot days, and the overall balance means less neck fatigue when you are looking up into the canopy for hours.
Ground crews use Protos helmets too, especially on felling and bucking jobs, though climbers are the main audience for the Integral Arborist model.
The fit system is designed for long days, and many climbers find it stays stable when looking up into the canopy for hours.
If you are switching from a helmet with bolt-on accessories, give yourself a few days to get used to the different feel and controls. The flip-up muffs and visor become second nature quickly.

There are several Protos models and limited edition colors, and Pfanner has released updated versions over the years, often called Protos 2 or newer generations. Make sure the exact model and its certifications match your employer's requirements, and check that replacement parts and accessories match your helmet generation.
Popular add-ons include neck protection and radio or Bluetooth hearing protection kits. Compare with the Kask Super Plasma and Petzl Vertex Vent if you prefer a modular setup.
Buy spare visor screens and earmuff cushions with your helmet. They wear faster than the shell, and keeping spares means you are not working with a scratched visor while you wait for parts.
Clean the shell and visor with mild soap and water, replace earmuff cushions when they flatten, and inspect the shell, chin strap and fit system regularly.

Choose a helmet that meets the standard your employer and ANSI Z133 require for the work you do, fit it per the manufacturer's instructions, and replace it after a significant impact or when it reaches the maker's service life.
Clean the visor gently; abrasive cleaners scratch the screen and make it harder to see clearly.

faq.q: Is the Protos helmet good for climbing?
faq.a: The Integral Arborist version is built for climbing with a chin strap. Other Protos versions may be aimed at ground forestry work, so check the model.

faq.q: What is the Protos 2?
faq.a: It is a common name for later generations of the Protos helmet. Check part compatibility between generations before ordering spares.

faq.q: Why is the Protos more expensive than other helmets?
faq.a: It includes integrated hearing and face protection that you would otherwise buy separately, and it is designed as one balanced system.

name: Buckingham Agility Saddle
title: Buckingham Agility Saddle: Buckingham Tree Saddle
meta: The Buckingham Agility is a Buckingham tree saddle built for climbers who move a lot in the canopy. Fit, features, who it suits and typical street price.
tagline: A Buckingham climbing saddle aimed at climbers who value freedom of movement.
summary: The Buckingham Agility saddle is a Buckingham tree saddle designed for climbers who move constantly in the canopy. It is built to let you twist, reach and limb walk without the saddle fighting you, while keeping the support you need for long hangs.
highlights: Designed for freedom of movement in the canopy
Bridge attachment for a wide working range
Padded waist and leg support for long days
Gear loops and side D-rings for lanyard and tools
Made by a long-established US saddle maker

p: Buckingham has been making climbing saddles in the US for a long time, and the Agility is aimed at climbers who spend their day moving: pruning wide crowns, limb walking and repositioning often. A bridge-style attachment lets your friction system travel side to side as you turn, so you are not twisting against a fixed point.
If you mostly do removals and hang in one spot, the support and seat may matter more to you than mobility. Compare with the Buckingham Buckcraft.

Mobility saddles are especially useful on large-crown pruning, where you spend a lot of time reaching out on limbs and rotating around the stem. Being able to turn without fighting the saddle saves energy over a full day.

Order the size that matches your waist and leg measurements, adjust it with the clothes you climb in, and hang test it before going aloft. Check stitching, webbing, bridge and D-rings before each climb.

A saddle is life-support equipment: buy one that meets the applicable standard, follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, inspect it before every climb and retire it when wear reaches the maker's limits. Get trained before you climb on any new system.
Look at gear loops and accessory options too. A saddle that carries your handsaw, carabiners and slings where you can reach them will make you more efficient.

faq.q: Is the Agility a good first saddle?
faq.a: It can be, if it fits well. Many new climbers are best served by trying on several saddles and getting guidance from a trainer.

faq.q: Is the bridge replaceable?
faq.a: Bridges are wear items on most modern saddles. Check Buckingham's instructions for replacement parts and procedures.

name: Buckingham Buckcraft Saddle
title: Buckingham Buckcraft: Classic Buckingham Tree Saddle
meta: The Buckingham Buckcraft is a classic Buckingham tree saddle with solid support for long days aloft. Features, fit, who it suits and typical street price.
tagline: A straightforward, supportive Buckingham saddle for working climbers.
summary: The Buckingham Buckcraft is a classic Buckingham tree saddle that puts support and durability first. It suits climbers who want a no-nonsense saddle that holds up to production work.
highlights: Supportive design for long hangs
Durable construction for production climbing
Side D-rings for lanyard work positioning
Gear loops for hardware and hand tools

p: Not every climber needs the newest design. The Buckcraft is a traditional saddle built to take abuse on removals, storm work and everyday pruning. It gives you solid support when you are hanging in one spot to cut and rig, and the side D-rings take a flip line or lanyard for positioning on the stem.
It is also a sensible saddle for crews outfitting several climbers. Compare with the more mobile Buckingham Agility.

A traditional saddle like this is also easier for newer climbers to learn on, because the connection points are simple and easy to see. That makes buddy checks and inspections faster on a busy morning.
Store it clean and dry, away from fuel and sunlight, between jobs.
Size it carefully, adjust it with the clothes you wear, and hang test before climbing. Inspect webbing, stitching, buckles and D-rings before each climb.

A saddle is life-support equipment: buy one that meets the applicable standard, follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, inspect it before every climb and retire it when wear reaches the maker's limits. Get trained before you climb on any new system.
Pair it with a quality flip line and climbing system. A saddle is only one part of the setup, and it should match the way you climb and the gear you already use.

faq.q: Is the Buckcraft good for removals?
faq.a: Its supportive, traditional design suits climbers who spend a lot of time hanging and cutting in one position.

faq.q: How do I pick a size?
faq.a: Use Buckingham's size chart for waist and legs, and try it on with your normal climbing clothes.

name: Buckingham Ergovation Saddle
title: Buckingham Ergovation Saddle for Arborist Climbers
meta: The Buckingham Ergovation saddle focuses on comfort and support for climbers who spend all day aloft. Features, fit notes and typical street price inside.
tagline: A comfort-focused Buckingham saddle for climbers who log long hours aloft.
summary: The Buckingham Ergovation is a climbing saddle built around comfort and support for climbers who spend most of the day aloft. Its ergonomic design spreads load across the waist and legs to reduce fatigue on long hangs.
highlights: Ergonomic design that spreads load
Built for long hours aloft
Bridge attachment for mobility
Gear loops and side D-rings
Buckingham build quality
