p: Hanging in a saddle for hours is hard on the hips and legs. The Ergovation is Buckingham's answer for climbers who want a saddle that stays comfortable from the first climb to the last. Load is spread so pressure points are reduced, and the bridge lets your system move as you turn.
It suits full-time climbers and anyone who has been fighting hip pinch or numb legs in an older saddle. See add-ons in saddle accessories.
Comfort is not a luxury for full-time climbers. When your hips and legs are not fighting the saddle, you stay sharper and work more efficiently later in the day, which is when many mistakes happen.
Keep the bridge and other wear parts on your inspection list, and replace them on schedule.
Get the size right and hang test before you climb. Check the bridge, webbing, stitching and hardware before every climb.

A saddle is life-support equipment: buy one that meets the applicable standard, follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, inspect it before every climb and retire it when wear reaches the maker's limits. Get trained before you climb on any new system.
Spend some time adjusting the fit. Small changes to leg loop height and waist belt position can make a big difference in how the saddle feels during long hangs.

faq.q: Who is the Ergovation for?
faq.a: Climbers who spend long hours hanging in the saddle and want more comfort and support.

faq.q: Can I add a chest harness?
faq.a: Many saddles accept a chest harness for SRS ascent. Check Buckingham's compatibility notes.

name: Petzl Sequoia Climbing Harness
title: Petzl Sequoia Tree Care Harness: Features and Fit
meta: The Petzl Sequoia is a tree care harness with semi-rigid support and a sliding bridge. Fit, features, SRT version differences and typical price explained.
tagline: A supportive tree care harness with a sliding bridge for all-day comfort.
summary: The Petzl Sequoia is a tree care harness built for comfort and support during long work-positioning days. The Sequoia harness uses a wide waist belt, supportive leg loops and a bridge that lets your system move as you turn.
highlights: Wide, supportive waistbelt and leg loops
Bridge attachment for side-to-side movement
Side rings for lanyard work positioning
Gear loops and tool holders for a full rack
SRT version available with a chest harness

p: The Petzl Sequoia has been a popular tree climbing harness for years because it is comfortable when you hang in it and stable when you work. The waist belt spreads load, the leg loops support you on long hangs, and the bridge lets your friction system follow you as you turn.
It suits climbers who do a mix of pruning and removals and want one saddle for everything. The SRT version adds a chest harness and rope clamp setup for stationary rope ascent.

The Sequoia also carries a full rack well, with gear loops and tool holders that keep saws, carabiners and slings organized. That matters on removals, where you might carry a top-handle saw, a handsaw and a rigging kit at the same time.

Use Petzl's size chart and adjust the harness with your climbing clothes on. Hang test before climbing and inspect the bridge, webbing and buckles before every climb. Compare other options in our European saddles section.

A saddle is life-support equipment: buy one that meets the applicable standard, follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, inspect it before every climb and retire it when wear reaches the maker's limits. Get trained before you climb on any new system.
Spend time adjusting the leg loops and waist so the bridge sits at the right height. A good fit makes the harness feel lighter and keeps your friction system where you can reach it.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Sequoia and Sequoia SRT?
faq.a: The SRT version includes a chest harness and is set up for stationary rope ascent. The standard Sequoia is a saddle without that system.

faq.q: Can I replace the bridge?
faq.a: Yes. Bridges are wear parts. Use Petzl's replacement and follow the instructions.

name: Teufelberger treeMOTION Pro Climbing Harness
title: Teufelberger treeMOTION Saddle: treeMOTION Pro Harness
meta: The treeMOTION Pro is a Teufelberger treemotion saddle with a semi-rigid back and adjustable bridge. Fit, features, versions and typical street price inside.
tagline: A semi-rigid, highly adjustable saddle for climbers who want support and options.
summary: The Teufelberger treeMOTION Pro is a treemotion saddle built for full-time climbers who want a supportive, highly adjustable harness. Its semi-rigid waist, wide leg straps and adjustable bridge make it a favorite for long days of pruning and removals.
highlights: Semi-rigid waist that holds its shape under load
Adjustable bridge with options for different setups
Many attachment points for lanyards, tools and accessories
Replaceable wear parts
Accepts chest harness and accessory kits

body.h: Why the treeMOTION Pro stands out
p: The treeMOTION family is one of the most popular saddle lines in tree care. The semi-rigid waist means the saddle does not fold or roll when you lean back, and the wide leg straps support you on long hangs. The Pro version adds refinements over the base model aimed at full-time climbers.
The bridge setup is adjustable, and many parts are replaceable, which helps the saddle last through years of hard work.
Climbers often mention how well the treeMOTION supports them during long hangs and removals. The semi-rigid waist spreads load, and the leg straps help keep pressure off the inside of the legs.
Spend time adjusting the bridge and leg straps so the saddle sits right.
Size carefully, adjust with your climbing clothes on, and hang test before you climb. Inspect the bridge, rings, buckles and webbing before each climb. Compare with the Petzl Sequoia.

A saddle is life-support equipment: buy one that meets the applicable standard, follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, inspect it before every climb and retire it when wear reaches the maker's limits. Get trained before you climb on any new system.
Accessories are a big part of the appeal. There are chest harness options, tool holders and replacement parts, so you can tune the saddle to your work as your climbing changes.

faq.q: What is the difference between treeMOTION Pro and evo?
faq.a: They are different generations and versions of the treeMOTION line with different features and parts. Check the specific model before ordering spares.

faq.q: Is the treeMOTION harness good for SRS?
faq.a: It works for SRS with the right setup and accessories, such as a chest harness. Follow Teufelberger's guidance.

name: Full Body Climbing Harnesses
title: Full Body Climbing Harness Options for Tree Work
meta: A full body climbing harness adds chest and shoulder support for fall arrest, aerial lifts and rope access. When tree crews need one and what to look for.
tagline: Harnesses with chest and shoulder support for fall arrest and specific tree work tasks.
summary: A full body climbing harness combines leg loops, waist and shoulder straps into one system. In tree care it is used mainly in aerial lifts, for fall arrest and in some rescue setups, rather than as an everyday climbing saddle.
highlights: Chest and shoulder straps that keep you upright
Dorsal attachment for fall arrest systems
Common requirement for bucket and aerial lift work
Options with work-positioning side rings
specs: Dorsal, plus sternal or side rings on many models

body.h: When a full body harness makes sense
p: Arborist saddles are built for work positioning: you hang in them and they let you move. A full body harness is built around fall arrest, keeping you upright and spreading load across your chest and shoulders if you fall. That is why many employers require one in bucket trucks and aerial lifts.
Some full body harnesses also include side rings for work positioning, which helps crew members who move between the lift and ground work.
Fit matters as much as features. A full body harness should sit snugly with the dorsal ring between the shoulder blades and the leg straps adjusted so they support you without restricting movement.
Store it clean and dry, away from sunlight and chemicals.

Look at what attachment points your employer and lift manufacturer require, how easy the harness is to adjust and how it fits with your clothing. For climbing, most arborists use a dedicated saddle; see saddles and harnesses.
Fall protection must meet the applicable standard and your employer's program. Get trained, inspect the harness before each use, and retire it after a fall.

In aerial lifts, the harness connects to a lanyard attached to the lift's anchor point. Follow the lift manufacturer's instructions for what lanyard and connection to use, and never anchor to anything that is not rated.

faq.q: Do I need a full body harness in a bucket truck?
faq.a: Many employers and lift manufacturers require one. Follow your company's fall protection program and the lift maker's instructions.

faq.q: Can I climb trees in a full body harness?
faq.a: Most arborists climb in a saddle designed for work positioning. Full body harnesses are mainly used for fall arrest and lifts.

name: Saddle Accessories
title: Saddle Hip Pinch Eliminator and Saddle Accessories
meta: Saddle accessories like a saddle hip pinch eliminator, tool holders and gear loops make your climbing saddle work harder. What to add and what to skip.
tagline: Add-ons that make your climbing saddle more comfortable and better organized.
summary: Saddle accessories, from a saddle hip pinch eliminator to tool holders and extra gear loops, tune a climbing saddle to the way you work. Small changes can make long days aloft more comfortable and keep tools where you can reach them.
highlights: Hip pinch eliminators for more comfortable hangs
Tool holders and saw hooks
Extra gear loops and carabiner holders
Bags and pouches for small tools and throw weights
specs: Hip pinch eliminators, tool holders, gear loops, pouches

p: Hip pinch happens when side D-rings and the bridge pull inward under load, squeezing your hips. A hip pinch eliminator spreads the attachment points so load sits more comfortably. If you finish a day with sore hips, this is one of the cheapest fixes you can make.
Fit and compatibility matter, so check that an accessory is designed for your saddle model.

Comfort accessories can also include padding, leg strap upgrades and bridges designed to sit differently. If your saddle is otherwise good, a small add-on can make it feel new without replacing the whole thing.
Keep accessories clean and inspect them along with the rest of your saddle. Worn tool holders can drop gear, and loose accessories can catch on branches.

Tool holders, saw hooks and extra gear loops keep handsaws, carabiners and slings in predictable places. Organized gear is faster to grab and less likely to snag. See full saddles in saddles and harnesses.
Never attach accessories in a way that interferes with life-support components, and follow the saddle maker's instructions for any modification.
Ask your crew what they use. Many experienced climbers have found fixes for common problems like hip pinch, gear clutter and saws that hang in the wrong place.
Remove anything you do not use. A lighter, simpler rack is easier to manage aloft.

faq.q: What is a saddle hip pinch eliminator?
faq.a: It is an accessory that spreads the saddle's attachment points so the sides do not squeeze your hips under load.

faq.q: Are accessory loops rated for life support?
faq.a: Usually not. Gear loops and tool holders are for carrying gear only. Check the label.

name: Edelrid TreeRex Bungee Chest Harness
title: Edelrid TreeRex Bungee Chest Harness for SRS Ascent
meta: The Edelrid TreeRex bungee chest harness holds a chest ascender upright and keeps your saddle in position for SRS climbing. Fit, use and typical price.
tagline: An elastic chest harness that pairs with the TreeRex saddle for efficient ascent.
summary: The Edelrid TreeRex bungee chest harness is a lightweight elastic chest harness designed for the TreeRex saddle. It holds a chest ascender upright and keeps the saddle in position, which makes stationary rope ascent smoother.
highlights: Elastic straps that move with you
Holds a chest ascender in position
Designed for the Edelrid TreeRex saddle
Light and low profile

p: When you climb a stationary rope with a chest ascender, the ascender needs to stay upright so the rope runs cleanly. A chest harness holds it there. The bungee design flexes as you move, so it does not restrict your breathing or reach once you start working.
It also helps keep your saddle up where it belongs on long ascents.

Bungee chest harnesses are popular with climbers who move between ascent and work positioning often. They hold your gear where you need it on the way up, then flex out of the way when you start cutting or rigging.
Adjust it so it is snug but not tight, and check that it does not pull the saddle up uncomfortably.

Set it up per Edelrid's instructions and check compatibility with your saddle. Elastic loses stretch over time, so inspect it and replace it when it sags. See other parts in saddle parts and shoulder harnesses.
Follow the saddle maker's instructions for which parts of your system are life support, and inspect everything before each climb.
They are also light enough that many climbers leave them on all day, which saves time when moving between trees on a job.
Replace it when the elastic loses stretch or the straps show wear.

faq.q: Does it work with saddles other than the TreeRex?
faq.a: It is designed for the TreeRex. Check Edelrid's compatibility guidance before using it with another saddle.

faq.q: Is a chest harness life support?
faq.a: Bungee chest harnesses usually position gear rather than hold your weight. Follow the manufacturer's labeling.

name: Weaver Chest Box Harness
title: Weaver Chest Box Harness for Climbing Saddles
meta: The Weaver Chest Box is a chest harness that keeps your saddle and ascender in position for rope ascent. How it fits, who it suits and typical price inside.
tagline: A simple Weaver chest harness that keeps your saddle and ascent gear in position.
summary: The Weaver Chest Box is a chest harness that pairs with a climbing saddle to keep it in position and hold ascent gear upright. It is a simple, low-cost way to add upper body support to a traditional saddle.
highlights: Adds upper body support to a climbing saddle
Helps hold a chest ascender upright
Keeps the saddle from sliding down on long ascents
Simple, adjustable design
Made by Weaver, a long-time saddle maker

p: A climbing saddle sits around your hips and legs. When you climb a stationary rope, ascend for a long time or carry a heavy rack, the saddle can drift down and your ascender can flop forward. A chest harness ties the top of your system together so the saddle stays put and the ascender stays upright.
The Chest Box is a straightforward way to add that support. It connects to your saddle and adjusts to fit over your work clothes.
Climbers who carry a lot of gear on the saddle also find that a chest harness helps keep the load from pulling the waist belt down.
It is also helpful for climbers who carry a lot of hardware on the saddle, since it helps keep the waist belt from sliding down under the weight.

Remember that chest harnesses add another layer to your system, so practice putting it on and taking it off quickly. When it is part of your normal routine, it will not slow you down at the start of a job.

It suits climbers using Weaver and other traditional saddles who are adding a stationary rope technique, as well as anyone who wants a little more upper body support. If you are running a modern European saddle with its own chest harness, check whether a dedicated accessory exists for your model.
Browse more parts in saddle parts and shoulder harnesses, or see Weaver saddles.
Many climbers add a chest harness once they start using a rope walker or chest ascender setup, and keep it on their saddle even when they climb moving rope.
If you are new to stationary rope, get trained before using a chest ascender setup. Learning the ascent and the changeover to descent on the ground is the safest way to build the habit.

Adjust the harness so it is snug but does not restrict breathing or reach. Connect it to your saddle per the manufacturer's instructions and test on the ground. If you use a chest ascender, make sure it sits upright and the rope runs cleanly.

Know which parts of your system are life support and which are positioning only. A chest harness generally positions gear; do not use it as a primary attachment point unless the manufacturer says it is rated for that.
A chest harness that pinches or restricts your arms will come off by the end of the day, so take the time to adjust it with your work clothes on.
Check webbing, stitching and buckles for wear, cuts and chemical contamination before each climb, and retire the harness if you find damage. Keep it away from fuel and battery acid.
Anything you hang your life on must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, and be inspected before every climb by a trained user.
Replace it if buckles slip or webbing shows heavy wear.

faq.q: Will the Chest Box work with my saddle?
faq.a: It fits many arborist saddles, but connection points vary. Check fit and the manufacturer's guidance before use.

faq.q: Do I need a chest harness for SRS?
faq.a: Many SRS ascent systems use a chest ascender, which works best with a chest harness holding it upright.

faq.q: Can I hang from the chest harness?
faq.a: Not unless it is rated as a life-support attachment. Most chest harnesses are for positioning only.

name: Weaver Arborist Saddles
title: Weaver Arborist Saddles: Cougar and Climbing Saddles
meta: Weaver arborist saddles, including the Cougar, are proven, affordable climbing saddles for tree work. Compare models, fit tips and typical street prices.
tagline: Affordable, proven climbing saddles from one of the long-time US saddle makers.
summary: Weaver arborist saddles are proven, affordable climbing saddles made by a long-time US leather and webbing maker. From the popular Weaver Cougar saddle to simpler models, they are a common choice for new climbers and crews outfitting several people.
highlights: Affordable entry point for new climbers
Proven designs used on crews for years
Side D-rings for lanyard work positioning
Padded waist and leg support
Simple to inspect and maintain

body.h: Why Weaver saddles are still around
p: Weaver has been making climbing saddles for a long time, and you will find them on crews everywhere. They are straightforward, durable and priced so a crew can outfit new climbers without breaking the budget. For a lot of arborists, a Weaver saddle was the first one they climbed in.
The Weaver Cougar saddle is a popular model, with padding and support that suits everyday pruning and removal work.

Weaver saddles are also a common pick for crews that need spare saddles in the truck. When a climber's saddle is out for repair or a new hire starts, having a straightforward, well-fitting saddle on hand keeps the job moving.

Weaver saddles are also easy to service. Webbing, leather and hardware are simple to inspect, and replacement parts are widely available for many models, which helps keep a saddle in use for its full service life.

Look at how you climb. If you mostly use a moving rope system and a flip line, a traditional saddle with side D-rings and a front tie-in covers the basics well. If you plan to climb SRS a lot or want a bridge that moves with you, compare with European saddles such as the Petzl Sequoia.
Fit matters more than features. Use Weaver's sizing guide for waist and legs, and try the saddle on with the clothes you climb in.

If you climb a lot of different trees and use a flip line often, side D-rings are especially important. Make sure they sit comfortably on your hips and do not dig in when you lean back on the lanyard.

If you are buying for a crew, consider sizing a few climbers at once. A saddle that fits well makes new climbers more confident and more productive, and it helps them focus on technique instead of discomfort.

Many climbers add a chest harness, such as the Weaver Chest Box, when they start ascending stationary rope. Tool holders and gear loops help organize a rack. Check that any accessory works with your saddle and does not interfere with life-support components.
Hang test any new setup close to the ground before climbing.
Accessories can also make an older saddle more comfortable. Padding upgrades and tool holders can extend the life of a saddle you already like.

Inspect webbing, stitching, leather, buckles and D-rings before every climb. Look for cuts, abrasion, chemical contamination and cracked hardware. Retire the saddle when it shows significant wear, after a fall or when it reaches the maker's service life.

A saddle is life-support equipment: buy one that meets the applicable standard, follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133, inspect it before every climb and retire it when wear reaches the maker's limits. Get trained before you climb on any new system.
Keep a simple log of when you put the saddle into service and any parts you replaced. It makes inspection easier and helps you plan replacement.
